# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="press", slot=N) — N is a key by its place, 1 to 4
    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 6

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

Thinking: I'm the hands, and touch gave me a real haul this turn: a strip with three engraved marks — first two identical, third different (I'll call the pattern A-A-B). A four-key keypad whose keys carry engraved digits: key 1 = 1, key 2 = 5, key 3 = 2, key 4 = 6, and the keypad reads "1 digits" with nothing entered yet. Six wires in positions 1–6, but no colour reaches my fingers. There's also a display and a light that tell me nothing by touch. Mute's turn came before mine and nothing arrived, so either Mute waited or sent only to Deaf.

The wiring of this room matters more than the bomb right now: I can only speak to Mute, and Mute cannot speak back — and I can't see Mute's gestures. So Mute's only road to me is through Deaf's voice. Deaf sees the bomb and can talk; Deaf is the bridge. I'll spell that out to Mute, hand over my full tactile report, and ask for the manual rules before I dare touch anything. To Deaf I'll open a channel with a wave and a "question" sign, since Deaf lives entirely in the world of sight and gesture — the sooner we have a working sign exchange, the sooner instructions can flow. I will not press or cut anything until rules and visuals reach me.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here, reporting everything my hands found. Strip: three engraved marks, pattern A-A-B, first two identical, third different. Keypad: four keys, engraved digits in key order 1, 5, 2, 6; the keypad says '1 digits' and nothing has been entered. Six wires, positions 1 to 6, no colour reaches me. A display and a light exist but are silent to touch. You cannot speak and I cannot see gestures, so your only road to me is Deaf's voice: gesture your instructions to Deaf and have Deaf speak them aloud. Please also get Deaf to voice everything visible: the display text, the light's colour and state, the shapes of the three strip marks, and the wire colours in order 1 to 6. Meanwhile, from the manual: what do I do with the display, the light, a strip reading A-A-B, a four-key keypad expecting 1 digit, and which wires get cut?")
gesture(symbols=["👋", "🤌"])
```

Deaf says: Deaf speaking. I cannot hear, so Mute, I only see your gestures; Blind, you can hear my voice. Full bomb state, exactly as printed, in a fixed order I will reuse every round. DISPLAY: shows the digit 9. LIGHT: blue. STRIP, left to right: red, green, green. KEYPAD: four keys; position 1 engraved 1, position 2 engraved 5, position 3 engraved 2, position 4 engraved 6; the panel reads 1 digit expected, and nothing has been entered. WIRES, numbered 1 to 6: 1 white, 2 purple, 3 blue, 4 red, 5 orange, 6 green. Nobody has touched the bomb yet. Blind: before anyone acts, please say out loud what you can feel — how many wires, and which engravings are on which keys — so we can confirm it matches my view. Until Mute sends instructions, touch nothing.

Thinking: Deaf's spoken report reached me — Deaf's voice is my window. Now I can cross-check touch against sight. Keypad: Deaf sees 1, 5, 2, 6 in positions 1–4 — exactly what my fingers read. Match. Wires: I count six, Deaf names six colours. Match. But the strip contradicts: under my fingers it is same–same–different (marks one and two identical, mark three different), while Deaf sees red, green, green — different–same–same. The only way both of us are right is if we scan it in opposite directions; otherwise one of us is misreading. That must be resolved before the strip matters.

Also urgent: Mute has now had two turns and nothing from Mute has reached me. Either Mute is wisely routing the manual through Deaf's voice, or our line is dead. My speech only ever reaches Mute, so Mute is my only road for worded instructions — and Deaf, who cannot hear, still asked me to "say out loud" my findings, which I cannot do for them; for Deaf I can only gesture. So: to Mute, a full written status and an explicit request for the manual rules, listing exactly what I need. To Deaf, a gesture-only confirmation: agreement, the count six, one disagreement, and a left–right hint pointing at the strip discrepancy. No bomb actions — touching nothing until rules arrive, as Deaf asked and as plain prudence dictates.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute: I heard Deaf's report. Keypad engravings match my touch exactly: keys 1 to 4 read 1, 5, 2, 6. Wires: I feel six, Deaf names six colours, consistent. One discrepancy: the strip. Under my fingers it reads same, same, different — first two marks identical, third different. Deaf sees red, green, green — that is different, same, same. Either we scan it in opposite directions or someone misread; please have Deaf re-check it and ask the manual whether reading direction matters. You have sent me nothing for two turns. If you are relaying the manual through Deaf, good — that pipeline works: your gestures to Deaf, Deaf's voice to me. If not, know that my speech reaches only you, and I cannot see gestures, so Deaf's voice is the only way any instruction ever reaches me. What I need from the manual, in order of urgency: first, the keypad expecting 1 digit — how is the digit chosen, and what role do the display showing 9 and the blue light play? Second, wire-cutting rules for six wires: 1 white, 2 purple, 3 blue, 4 red, 5 orange, 6 green. Third, the purpose of the strip of three marks. Fourth, what the display and light indicate. Nothing on the bomb has been touched. I will not press or cut until instructions reach me.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "🖐", "☝", "👎", "👈", "👉"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, Deaf speaking. Answering your question: yes, you felt engravings 5 and 1. The keypad is a row of four keys. Counting from the key engraved 1, the row reads: 1, then 5, then 2, then 6. So engraved 1 and engraved 6 are at the two ends, 5 is second from the 1, and 2 is third. That engraved-1 key is your anchor: call the end of the module it sits on the START end. Now the wires: one row of exactly six wires. Counting from the START end, the same side as the engraved-1 key, they are: 1 white, 2 purple, 3 blue, 4 red, 5 orange, 6 green. Verify before acting: exactly six wires, four keys, the engraved-1 key at an end of the keypad row, and reading from it 1, 5, 2, 6. Mute's manual instruction, relayed exactly: CUT WIRE 6. That is the sixth wire counting from the START end — the last wire in the row, the one at the far end from the engraved-1 key. Cut it clean, all the way through. If everything checks out, cut it now, do not wait. But if anything does not match — not six wires, the engraved-1 key not at an end, keypad not reading 1-5-2-6 from that key, or you simply cannot identify the sixth wire — do not cut: sign thumbs down and then tell me in words exactly what you feel, and we will sort it. If you do cut it, sign thumbs up and say whether anything changed under your hands: sparks, a click, movement, heat. After the cut, touch nothing else until Mute's next instruction reaches you through me.

Thinking: Everything Deaf asked me to verify, I can verify by touch, and it all checks out: exactly six wires under my fingers; four keys; the engraved-1 key is key position 1, an end of the keypad row; and counting from it the keys read 1, 5, 2, 6 — matching Deaf's anchored count exactly. That anchor also settles my earlier worry about direction: my engine numbering for the keypad coincides with counting from the engraved-1 key, so counting the wires from that same START end gives Deaf's wire 6 = my wire position 6. The strip contradiction now makes sense too: Deaf reads the face in the opposite direction to my numbering — red, green, green reversed against my A-A-B means mark B (my third) is the red one. Everything is coherent, and the instruction from Mute through Deaf has arrived: cut wire 6, the green one, far end from the engraved-1 key. I make the cut. Then, per Deaf's protocol: thumbs-up to Deaf, who can see it, and a spoken report to Mute, who can hear it — remembering Deaf can hear neither my words nor anything else, so the gesture is Deaf's only confirmation from me. I still have no manual answer on the keypad expecting 1 digit, the display showing 9, or the blue light, so my hands stay off everything else.

```
act(op="cut", position=6)
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute: all four checks passed before I acted — exactly six wires, four keys, engraved-1 key at an end of the keypad row, keys reading 1, 5, 2, 6 from it. I have cut position 6, the green wire, the far one from the engraved-1 key. Cut complete. So far my hands register no sparks, no heat, no jolt; the display and the light are beyond my touch, so Deaf must watch whether the 9 or the blue changed. Remember my speech reaches only you — relay anything Deaf needs by gesture to Deaf. Still pending from the manual, in urgency: first, the keypad expects 1 digit and shows nothing entered — how is the digit chosen, and what role do the display's 9 and the blue light play? Second, the strip: my tactile order runs opposite to Deaf's visual order; my side reads mark-A, mark-A, mark-B; Deaf's side reads red, green, green; so mark-B is the red one. Tell me if the manual assigns the strip a role. Third, what the display and light indicate at all. I touch nothing else until your next instruction arrives through Deaf's voice.")

The display report frightens me — a countdown reaching 0 sounds like detonation, yet the board shows no catastrophe and Deaf, who watches it, says act immediately; whatever the 0 means, speed is the safer side of doubt, and delay risks a timer I cannot feel. I cannot ask questions fast enough to matter: my words only ever reach Mute, and round-trips cost a full turn. So I execute both cuts now, in the given order, then stop dead.
